# Blender

Every scene is one Python script that builds everything from an empty file. You never edit a live Blender session: you change the script, rebuild, render, look at the image, and repeat. `scripts/bl.py` runs that loop; `assets/scene_template.py` is a verified starting scene.

Throughout, `SKILL` is the directory containing this file, and `bl` means `python3 SKILL/scripts/bl.py`.

## 1. Check the tools

Run `bl probe`. It prints the Blender and ffmpeg it found. If Blender is missing, ask the user for its path and set `BLENDER=/path/to/blender`. If ffmpeg is missing, ask the user to install it; stills still render but contact sheets and MP4s do not.

Never open, modify, or connect to a Blender instance the user already has running. Other agents may be using it. All work runs in separate background processes.

## 2. Decide what to build

From the brief, write down in a few lines: the hero subject, what moves and why, the environment, the shot list (two to six camera keys with frames), duration, and resolution. Ask only if the subject itself is unclear.

When the brief is open, choose a subject whose correctness sells it: a mechanism whose parts genuinely interact, light doing something physical, or real structure built from parameters. One hero, a supporting environment, and a camera move that reveals scale beat many unrelated objects. Scale for readability, not realism: a planet the size it would really be is invisible.

## 3. Write the scene script

Copy `SKILL/assets/scene_template.py` into the project as `<name>.py`. Keep its helpers, world, camera rig, render, and compositor sections; replace the SUBJECT section.

- Generate geometry from parameters with `bmesh` (profiles, counts, radii), and give every object a stable name.
- Put all motion on keyframes at the first and last frame (`spin`) or in Geometry Nodes driven by `Scene Time`. Derive related motion from one master value so parts stay consistent, e.g. gear rates from tooth ratios.
- Where parts could collide or interpenetrate, check the clearance in the script and print it; fix the layout before rendering.
- Before using anything the template does not already use (new node types, compositor nodes, geometry nodes, volumes, animation of node values), read `SKILL/references/blender-5-api.md`. Read it too when a build fails with an unknown identifier or attribute.

## 4. Iterate on stills

Run `bl stills <name>.py --frames <first>,<middle>,<last> --preview --out tmp/stills`. It builds the scene, saves `tmp/stills/scene.blend`, renders the frames at half resolution, and writes `tmp/stills/contact.png`. If it fails, it prints the Python traceback: fix the script and rerun. Do not work around a traceback by catching it.

Open `contact.png` and judge it against this list, worst problem first:

1. Exposure: frame not washed out or crushed. Haze density above about 0.01, or strong lights inside haze, fog the whole frame.
2. Metals read as metal. If they look black or flat grey, they have nothing to reflect: the world must light them (the template's studio world) and the world `Volume` socket must stay empty. A large floor or wall that looks flat grey is mirroring that world: raise its roughness, darken it, or move the world's bright band higher.
3. Glows are coloured, not white. Lower emission strength and saturate the ramp; bloom supplies the glow.
4. The subject is readable at this size, and the frame has a clear focal point and depth-of-field focus on it.
5. Nothing interpenetrates, floats unintentionally, or ends in a visible edge (floor, haze box, backdrop).

Once the frame is free of defects, judge it against the quality the brief asks for. A quick draft or a technical check can stop here. For anything described as polished, impressive, or for showing to others, keep going until all of these hold:

- The hero has the detail its real counterpart would: bevelled edges, joints and fasteners that connect, wear or variation in the material. No part reads as a bare primitive, and nothing that should connect floats.
- Lighting has a direction and contrast: a clear key, a rim or separation light, and shadow shaping the forms rather than flat, even light.
- The environment supports the subject without competing: a surface, a backdrop, or atmosphere that gives depth, and no empty grey field.
- The camera move has a purpose (reveal, follow, or orbit toward a hero angle), with focus on the subject.

Fix the one or two biggest problems, rerun, and look again. Expect three to six passes. A command that exits cleanly proves nothing about how the image looks; only the image does.

## 5. Check the camera path

Run `bl stills <name>.py --frames <eight evenly spaced frames, including each camera key> --preview --out tmp/path`. Open the contact sheet and check that the camera never passes through geometry, never loses the subject, and never frames empty space during a move. Move the camera keys or look-at targets and repeat until every frame holds.

## 6. Estimate and render

Run `bl stills <name>.py --frames <middle> --out tmp/full` without `--preview` to render one full-quality frame. It prints `BL_FRAME <n> <seconds>`. Multiply by the frame count for the render time. If it exceeds about 45 minutes, tell the user the estimate and offer lower resolution, fewer samples, or a shorter shot before starting.

Run `bl animate <name>.py --out tmp/animate` as a background process (it can take a long time). Wait for it to finish; do not report completion before the MP4 exists. Check progress by counting `tmp/animate/frames/f_*.png`. If it stops early, rerun the same command: it resumes from the frames already on disk. When it finishes it encodes `tmp/animate/<name>.mp4` and writes `tmp/animate/video_contact.png`.

Open `video_contact.png`. If a frame shows a defect, fix the script and rerun from step 4. Delete `tmp/animate/frames` before rerendering, or unchanged frames will be skipped.

## 7. Deliver

Copy the MP4 and `scene.blend` to where the user wants them, and commit the scene script if the project uses git. Report the paths, the render time, and any defect you saw but did not fix.

If the user wants to inspect the scene, run `bl open <file>.blend`. It always starts a new Blender instance and never loads the file into one that is already running.
